entries.question: How many animals of each kind did Noah take into the ark?
entries.summary: Genesis 6:19 and 7:8-9 and 7:14-15 say two of every sort — male and female — went into the ark. Genesis 7:2 says Noah was to take clean animals by sevens. The Pentateuch's flood narrative gives two different animal counts within the same chapter.
entries.commentary: The apologist harmonization is that the two-of-every-kind is the general rule and the seven-of-clean-kinds is a sub-specification for kosher animals used in the post-flood sacrifice of Genesis 8:20. Archer, Walton, and Hamilton all run this. It is a coherent reading if you accept it at face value — God commanded two as the baseline and seven as an extra allotment of clean animals for sacrifice. But the critical read sees what the harmonization is papering over. Richard Friedman and Joel Baden have demonstrated repeatedly that Genesis 6-9 is the cleanest example of Pentateuchal source weaving in the entire Torah. The Priestly source has two animals of every kind (6:19; 7:15-16) because P writes before the Sinai legislation and refuses to acknowledge clean/unclean distinctions prior to Leviticus; ritual categories are a post-Sinai innovation for P. The Yahwistic source has seven pairs of clean animals and one pair of unclean (7:2-3) because J has no such theological scruple — the distinction predates Moses as a folk category. Gary Rendsburg and David Carr both trace the way these two strands interleave with different vocabulary (Yahweh vs. Elohim), different chronologies, and different animal counts. The harmonization requires treating the text as one unified narrative; the evidence shows two narratives stitched together. The counts don't contradict each other within one source — they contradict because two sources are present. This is arguably the single most persuasive case for the Documentary Hypothesis in the entire Hebrew Bible.
entries.scholarship: Baden, Joel S. *The Composition of the Pentateuch: Renewing the Documentary Hypothesis*. New Haven: Yale University Press, 2012 — ch. on the flood as Documentary test case. Friedman, Richard Elliott. *The Bible with Sources Revealed*. San Francisco: HarperSanFrancisco, 2003. Carr, David M. *Reading the Fractures of Genesis*. Louisville: Westminster John Knox, 1996. Rendsburg, Gary A. *The Redaction of Genesis*. Winona Lake: Eisenbrauns, 1986 — though Rendsburg argues for unity, his analysis of the seams is useful. Westermann, Claus. *Genesis 1-11: A Continental Commentary*. Minneapolis: Fortress, 1994.

entries.question: Did everyone (except for Noah and his family) die in the flood?
entries.summary: Genesis 7:21-23 insists that every living thing outside the ark perished, yet Genesis 6:4 and Numbers 13:33 have the Nephilim — the giant offspring of the 'sons of God' — still walking around after the flood in the days of Moses. The text cannot have both a hermetic global extinction and a post-flood population of antediluvian monsters.
entries.commentary: Apologists typically read Genesis 6:4 to mean the Nephilim existed 'in those days, and also after that' as a second, independent giant lineage that arose after the flood — Kenneth Mathews and Victor Hamilton both push this harmonization, treating Numbers 13:33 as a reputational echo or a later Anakim group unrelated to the pre-flood giants. The problem is that Numbers 13:33 explicitly identifies the Anakim as descended from the Nephilim, and the scouts are terrified specifically because these are the same kind of beings. The deeper issue is source-critical. Gen 6:1-4 is a J fragment that many scholars (Friedman, Speiser, Westermann) read as an etiological note about heroic beings still known in Israel's memory, appended to a Priestly flood frame that insists on total destruction. The redactor stitched two incompatible traditions together: the cosmic do-over of P and the older Yahwistic giant-lore. Ronald Hendel's work on the Nephilim traditions shows Second Temple literature (1 Enoch, Jubilees) solved the problem by inventing demonology — the flood killed the giants' bodies but their spirits became demons — precisely because readers noticed the incoherence. If you have to invent a whole demon cosmology to fix the story, the story has a problem.

entries.question: How long did the flood last?
entries.summary: Genesis 7:17 says the flood was on the earth for forty days, while Genesis 7:24 and 8:3 say the waters prevailed for a hundred and fifty days. Two different numerical frames for the same event sit side by side in the same chapter.
entries.commentary: The standard harmonization, pressed by Gleason Archer and John Walton, is that the forty days refers only to the rain falling while the one hundred and fifty days refers to the total time the waters prevailed before receding. That reading is possible at the surface, but it ignores why there are two incompatible chronologies in the first place. Critical scholarship since Wellhausen has treated Genesis 6-9 as a textbook example of source stitching: the Yahwist (J) tradition uses a forty-day schema with seven clean pairs of animals and a seven-day warning (Gen 7:4, 7:10, 7:12, 8:6), while the Priestly (P) tradition operates on a precise 150-day cycle keyed to dated months and one pair of each kind (Gen 7:11, 7:24, 8:3-4, 8:13-14). Friedman's color-coded reconstruction in The Bible with Sources Revealed separates the two strands cleanly, and each reads as a coherent flood story on its own. The contradiction isn't a logical puzzle to solve — it's the literary signature of a redactor splicing two independent flood accounts. Treating the numbers as sequential rather than parallel is a harmonization move that presupposes a unity the text does not display.

entries.question: How long was the ark afloat?
entries.summary: Genesis 8:4 has the ark resting on Ararat in the seventh month, while Genesis 8:5 says the mountaintops only became visible in the tenth month. An ark cannot be resting on a mountain three months before the mountain pokes above the water.
entries.commentary: Mathews and Hamilton try to smooth this by arguing the ark came to rest on a submerged high peak whose summit wasn't yet visible, with the tops of lower mountains becoming visible three months later. It's physically possible as a single image, but it strains the plain sequence of the narrative, which treats 'mountains of Ararat' and 'tops of the mountains' as parallel reference points rather than one specific peak versus a range. The cleaner explanation is again source-critical. The dated notices in Genesis 8:4-5, 13-14 belong to the Priestly schema, and P's dating system operates on a liturgical calendar whose internal logic doesn't fully smooth into a naturalistic travelogue. Speiser in the Anchor Bible commentary already flagged the awkwardness of reading these dates as a continuous eyewitness log. The point isn't that a reader can't construct a physical scenario — the point is that the text is a theologically structured chronology, not an engineering report, and forcing it to behave like one generates incoherence the original authors didn't care about.

entries.question: When did the earth dry after the flood?
entries.summary: Genesis 8:13 declares the waters dried up on the first day of the first month, but Genesis 8:14 puts the earth's drying on the twenty-seventh day of the second month — almost two months later. The same narrative gives two different drying dates.
entries.commentary: Archer's standard move is to distinguish 'the waters were dried up from off the earth' (8:13) as referring to surface water evaporating from the mud from 'the earth was dried' (8:14) as the ground becoming firm enough to walk on. Hebrew does use different verbal forms here (charav in 8:13, yavesh in 8:14), and apologists run with that distinction. The problem is that this reads a precise technical geology into two verses that sit in the middle of the Priestly dating scheme and are otherwise formulaic date-stamps in a liturgical calendar. Friedman and Baden note that the dated notices in Gen 7-8 follow a symmetrical P calendar that is more about ritual numerology than narrative reportage. The gap between the dates probably reflects the editorial stitching of P's ceremonial timeline, not a fine-grained distinction between damp topsoil and bone-dry substrate. Treating these as two stages of a single drying process is doable — it's just not what the Priestly author was tracking.

entries.question: Will God curse the earth?
entries.summary: Genesis 8:21 has God swear in his heart never again to curse the ground because of humanity, yet Isaiah 24:1-6 announces a curse that devours the earth and Malachi 4:6 warns that Yahweh will come and smite the earth with a curse. The promise is issued and then revoked.
entries.commentary: Apologists like Archer and John Oswalt distinguish two Hebrew words — qalal in Gen 8:21 (often translated 'curse') and different terms in Isaiah 24 (alah) and Malachi 4:6 (cherem-adjacent language) — arguing the Genesis oath is narrowly about the flood-style cursing of the ground's agricultural fertility, while the prophetic curses are covenantal judgments on specific populations. That lexical point has force in the weeds, but it doesn't rescue the plain reading. Genesis 8:21 explicitly promises no more universal earth-destruction tied to human wickedness ('I will not again curse the ground any more for man's sake... neither will I again smite any more every thing living'), and Isaiah 24's cosmic-scale devastation is framed in exactly those terms — the earth emptied, polluted by its inhabitants, its covenant broken. Brevard Childs and Joseph Blenkinsopp both read Isaiah 24-27 (the so-called 'Isaiah Apocalypse') as deliberately echoing and reversing Noahic themes. The author of Isaiah 24 wasn't trying to respect Gen 8:21 — he was announcing a new judgment that overrides it. That's not harmonization; that's the Bible talking back to itself.

entries.question: Is it OK to eat blood?
entries.summary: The Priestly and Deuteronomic Torah absolutely forbids eating blood as a perpetual statute (Gen 9:4; Lev 3:17; 7:26-27; 17:10-14; 19:26; Deut 12:16, 23), and the apostolic decree in Acts 15 reaffirms that prohibition for Gentile Christians. John 6:53-56, however, has Jesus commanding that his followers eat his flesh and drink his blood to have eternal life. The Torah bans blood-drinking outright; the Johannine Jesus makes it the condition of salvation.
entries.commentary: The standard Catholic and apologetic response is that John 6 is either symbolic (so Calvin, many Protestants) or sacramental (so Raymond Brown, in a qualified way) — either way, not a violation of the Levitical ban, since the eucharistic referent is Jesus' flesh and blood, not a prohibited animal. Craig Blomberg and D. A. Carson argue the Levitical prohibition targeted ritual slaughter of animals within Israel's purity system, not the sacramental participation in a salvific death. That defense works for internal Christian theology but collapses when you pull back. The whole point of Leviticus 17:11 is that 'the life of the flesh is in the blood, and I have given it to you upon the altar to make an atonement for your souls' — blood is forbidden precisely because it is the site of atonement and belongs to God. John 6 presses the exact same logic in reverse: the disciples must drink the blood because it is the site of atonement. Klawans and Milgrom both note how shocking John 6 would sound to a first-century Jewish ear — John's narrator even stages that shock ('Many therefore of his disciples, when they had heard this, said, This is an hard saying'). The harmonization papers over a real theological rupture. And Acts 15:20 shows the apostolic church itself still upholding the Torah ban while presumably also practicing the eucharist, which either means they didn't read John 6 literally or they hadn't encountered it yet (John being the latest canonical gospel). Take your pick.

entries.question: Will God flood the earth again?
entries.summary: Genesis 9:11-15 gives an unqualified covenantal 'no' — God swears never again to flood the earth, with the rainbow as the binding sign. Nahum 1:8, however, describes God using 'an overrunning flood' to make an utter end of his enemies' place.
entries.commentary: Hamilton and Walton argue that Nahum's 'overrunning flood' is a localized judgment metaphor directed at Nineveh, not a repeat of the Genesis deluge, and that the Noachic covenant specifically pertains to a global hydrological event. That harmonization works at a technical level — Nahum is clearly poetic threat-language against Assyria — and honestly, this is one of the weaker contradictions in the SAB catalog. The critical observation is subtler: Nahum uses flood imagery precisely because it still carries divine-judgment freight in Israel's theological vocabulary, which means Gen 9:11's covenant hasn't actually retired the metaphor of God-as-flooder. More pointedly, 2 Peter 3:5-7 explicitly envisions a future cosmic destruction that parallels the flood ('the world that then was, being overflowed with water, perished: but the heavens and the earth, which are now... reserved unto fire'), transposing the Noahic extinction into fire rather than respecting its finality. The theological promise of Gen 9 gets relitigated in later apocalyptic texts. Nahum isn't the sharpest edge of that tension, but it's an edge.

entries.question: Are we punished for the sins of others?
entries.books_in_tension: Deuteronomy, 2 Kings, 2 Chronicles, Jeremiah, Ezekiel, Romans
entries.summary: Romans 5:12 has Paul teach that death passed upon all humanity because of Adam's single sin — the archetypal transgenerational punishment. Deuteronomy 24:16, 2 Kings 14:6, Jeremiah 31:29-30, and Ezekiel 18:20 insist the opposite: each person dies for his own sin and no one bears the iniquity of another.
entries.commentary: The classical reformed harmonization, pressed by Doug Moo and John Murray, is that Romans 5 teaches federal headship — Adam sinned as humanity's representative, so we don't bear his guilt directly but inherit the corruption and death that flow from it, while Deuteronomy 24 and Ezekiel 18 govern human judicial procedures, not God's metaphysical accounting. That distinction is theologically sophisticated but it does not actually resolve the tension on the ground. Ezekiel 18:20 is explicit that 'the soul that sinneth, it shall die; the son shall not bear the iniquity of the father.' It frames this as Yahweh's own judgment principle, not a human courtroom rule, and it directly contradicts the older Exodus 20:5 formula about visiting iniquity 'unto the third and fourth generation.' Joel Kaminsky's Corporate Responsibility in the Hebrew Bible traces this exact tension — the Hebrew Bible contains both corporate and individualist streams of moral accounting, and texts like Ezekiel 18 and Deuteronomy 24:16 press back against the older corporate-retribution framework visible in Exodus 20:5 (even if, as Kaminsky argues, the shift is less a clean revolution than a reweighting). Paul then inherits and radicalizes the older corporate theology via Adam, precisely the model Ezekiel was trying to bury. Romans 5:12-19 isn't a minor doctrinal gloss — it's the theological engine of original sin, and it runs directly against Ezekiel's 'the son shall not bear the iniquity of the father.' You can privilege one stream over the other, but you cannot pretend they are saying the same thing.

entries.question: Who was Sheba's father?
entries.summary: The Table of Nations and its parallels give three different fathers for a man named Sheba: Raamah (Gen 10:7; 1 Chr 1:9), Jokshan son of Abraham and Keturah (Gen 25:3; 1 Chr 1:32), and Joktan son of Eber (Gen 10:26-28; 1 Chr 1:20-22). Three genealogies, three fathers.
entries.commentary: The obvious harmonization, offered by Kidner and Mathews, is that 'Sheba' is simply a name three different ancient Near Eastern tribes independently used — the Cushite Sheba of Gen 10:7, the Abrahamic Sheba of Gen 25, and the Joktanide Sheba of Gen 10:26 are different people from different clans who share a common name. That's not crazy. The name Sheba is well attested across ancient South Arabian inscriptions as a regional ethnonym, and ethnic names getting recycled across unrelated lineages is normal. But this move only works if you treat Genesis 10 as a sober ethnographic catalog rather than what it actually is — a theological map of the known world organized into a 70-nation schema. Westermann, Cassuto, and more recently John Day have shown that Genesis 10 functions as a literary-ideological document whose genealogies are overlapping claims about the relationship of peoples to Israel, with different traditions preserving different political alignments. The three Shebas aren't three people — they're three attempts by different tradents to locate the Sabean/Arabian peoples within the genealogical imagination of Israel. Treating this as 'three different men with the same name' is a harmonization that turns a political text into a phonebook.

entries.question: Where was Abraham buried?
entries.summary: Genesis 25:8-10 has Abraham buried in the cave of Machpelah near Hebron, on a plot he purchased from Ephron the Hittite. Stephen's speech in Acts 7:15-16 relocates Abraham's tomb to Shechem and has him purchasing the plot from 'the sons of Emmor the father of Sychem' — the tomb Jacob later buys in Genesis 33:19.
entries.commentary: This is one of the cleaner factual contradictions in the New Testament. Apologists like Darrell Bock and F. F. Bruce argue that Stephen's speech is a rapid-fire summary conflating two purchase stories — Abraham's at Hebron (Gen 23) and Jacob's at Shechem (Gen 33:19) — and that either Luke is accurately reporting Stephen's memory lapse in a charged speech, or Stephen is using a telescoping rhetorical device. Either version concedes the factual error; it just relocates blame. Ernst Haenchen's classic Anchor Bible-era work on Acts and more recent commentaries by Richard Pervo and Craig Keener all acknowledge the historical inaccuracy and debate only whether Luke was aware of it. The move of saying 'Luke is quoting Stephen, so Luke isn't wrong even if Stephen is' is the apologetic playbook's way of preserving inerrancy by pushing the error one level down. But that's not what inerrancy means on any robust definition — if the speech is wrong on plain historical facts that Acts presents without correction, the text transmits an error. Apologists who accept Stephen's telescoping have quietly accepted that biblical narration is not uniformly accurate; they just don't phrase it that way.

entries.question: Who was Dedan's father?
entries.summary: Genesis 10:7 and 1 Chronicles 1:9 list Dedan as the son of Raamah in the Cushite/Hamite line, while Genesis 25:3 and 1 Chronicles 1:32 list Dedan as the son of Jokshan in the Abrahamic/Keturite line. The genealogies give two fathers for the same ethnonym.
entries.commentary: Same structural problem as the Sheba contradiction in id=49, and the same harmonization is available: these are two distinct Dedanites from two distinct clans. Mathews and Kidner take exactly that route, pointing out that Dedan is attested as an important North Arabian trade center and it's plausible that two tribes with overlapping territory carried the same ethnonym. Fair enough — but the tell that this is about genealogy-as-geography, not genealogy-as-biology, is that Sheba and Dedan appear together in both lists. The same paired names get relocated from the Hamite line to the Abrahamic line across traditions. Ronald Hendel and John Day read this as the Chronicler and the Yahwist preserving competing political maps of North Arabia. When the Priestly editor compiles both into the canonical shape, he gets two contradictory patrilines side by side and doesn't bother to reconcile them. The apologetic 'two different people with the same name in the same territory doing the same trade' requires an improbable coincidence across multiple name-pairs. Parsimony favors: the tradition had multiple conflicting ethnographic catalogs and the final redactor preserved all of them.

entries.question: Who was the father of Uz, Hul, and Gether?
entries.summary: Genesis 10:23 lists Uz, Hul, and Gether as sons of Aram (making them Aram's generation, great-grandsons of Shem). 1 Chronicles 1:17, however, lists the same three names as direct sons of Shem — skipping Aram entirely.
entries.commentary: Kidner and Mathews note that 1 Chronicles 1 frequently collapses intermediate generations in its genealogical lists, and this is a widely acknowledged pattern in Chronicles — abbreviated genealogies that skip generations to compress lineage while preserving key nodes. Gary Knoppers' Anchor Bible commentary on 1 Chronicles makes that case at length, and honestly it is the best reading of the Chronicler's technique. The contradiction, if it's one, is mild: Chronicles is not claiming these are biological sons of Shem, he's naming them under Shem's genealogical umbrella. However, the harmonization concedes the key point: 1 Chronicles 1:17 as printed — 'the sons of Shem; Elam, and Asshur, and Arphaxad, and Lud, and Aram, and Uz, and Hul, and Gether, and Meshech' — reads Aram as one item in a list that continues with names that are, per Genesis 10, Aram's children. The flat-list syntax is misleading unless you already know Genesis 10. Some manuscripts of the LXX and the parallel in the MT are textually unstable here, suggesting later scribes noticed the tension. The Chronicler was working from a Genesis 10 tradition and produced a telegraphed list; the result reads as a contradiction at face value even if a sympathetic reader can reconstruct his method.

entries.question: How many languages were there before the Tower of Babel was built?
entries.summary: Genesis 11:1 declares that 'the whole earth was of one language, and of one speech' before God confounds speech at Babel. Genesis 10:5, 20, 31 — one chapter earlier — already describes the descendants of Noah as divided 'every one after his tongue' in multiple languages.
entries.commentary: Walton and Mathews offer the standard narrative-arrangement defense: Genesis 10 is a topical anticipation of the post-Babel diversity, and the events of Genesis 11 are chronologically prior to the linguistic dispersal described in chapter 10. In other words, Genesis 10 is written with hindsight, presenting the nations in their later diversified state, while Genesis 11 flashes back to tell you how they got that way. That ordering is coherent, and it's a common feature of ancient Near Eastern narrative to give a summary outcome before the explanatory flashback. Fine as far as it goes. But the source-critical reading is sharper. Genesis 10 (largely P, with a J insertion in 10:8-19) and the Babel narrative (Gen 11:1-9, J) are independent traditions about national origins that the Priestly compiler placed side-by-side. P's Table of Nations assumes linguistic diversity is a feature of how God structured the post-flood world, while the J narrative of Babel treats linguistic diversity as a punishment for human hubris. These are theologically incompatible origin stories for the same phenomenon. The 'narrative recapitulation' harmonization papers over that deeper conflict. Speiser, Westermann, and Friedman all read the juxtaposition as a classic redactional seam.

entries.question: Who was the father of Salah?
entries.summary: Genesis 10:24 and 11:12 both have Arphaxad directly fathering Salah. Luke 3:35-36 inserts a generation — 'Salah, which was the son of Cainan, which was the son of Arphaxad' — making Cainan an intermediate ancestor.
entries.commentary: This is one of the cleanest textual-critical contradictions in the whole enterprise. Apologists like Archer and Glenn Morton argue Luke is following the Greek Septuagint, which does include a second Cainan at Gen 10:24 (LXX), and thus Luke's genealogy reflects a legitimate variant textual tradition. That's empirically true — the LXX of Gen 10:24 and 11:12-13 does insert Cainan. The problem is that the name appears to be a scribal expansion in the LXX tradition that has no support in the Masoretic Hebrew, the Samaritan Pentateuch, or the Qumran Genesis fragments. Emanuel Tov's textual-critical work treats the LXX Cainan as a secondary addition designed to harmonize generational counts. So the apologist either has to say (a) Luke faithfully recorded a corrupt Greek text, which means scripture transmits a genealogical error with divine authority, or (b) the MT is itself defective and the LXX preserved the original — which almost no critical textual scholar endorses and which would require rewriting every Hebrew genealogy. Either way, Luke 3:36 is in direct conflict with the Hebrew text of Genesis on a basic paternity question. The LXX defense doesn't eliminate the contradiction, it just moves which Bible contains it.

entries.question: How old was Terah when he died?
entries.summary: Genesis 11:32 states directly that Terah died in Haran at age 205. But Gen 11:26 says Terah was 70 when Abram was born, Gen 12:4 says Abram left Haran at 75, and Acts 7:4 says Abram only left after his father had died — which would put Terah's death at age 145, not 205.
entries.commentary: The standard harmonization, pressed by F. F. Bruce and Darrell Bock, is that Gen 11:26 ('Terah lived seventy years, and begat Abram, Nahor, and Haran') doesn't mean Abram was born when Terah was 70 — it means Terah began fathering sons at 70, and Abram was actually the youngest, born when Terah was 130. Then when Terah died at 205, Abram was 75 and left Haran, and Acts 7:4 fits. That reconstruction is clever but requires reading a highly specific chronological gloss into a formulaic 'X lived N years and begat Y' template that elsewhere in Genesis does indicate the age at the named son's birth (as in the Shem genealogies of Gen 11:10ff). You can't run the formula one way for the Shem list and a different way for Gen 11:26. More tellingly, the Samaritan Pentateuch actually reads Terah's lifespan as 145 years at Gen 11:32 — a textual variant that looks like an early attempt to fix exactly this contradiction. Emanuel Tov and James VanderKam both treat the Samaritan reading as a harmonizing correction. That's the diagnostic: the text was already generating contradiction-anxiety in antiquity, and the Samaritan scribes tried to patch it. Luke, writing in Greek, knew the traditional reading and went with it — creating a conflict with MT Genesis that apologists have been trying to solve for 1900 years.

entries.question: How old was Abraham when Ishmael was born?
entries.summary: Genesis 16:16 says plainly that Abraham was 86 when Ishmael was born. But if you stack Gen 11:26 (Terah was 70 when Abram was born), Acts 7:4 (Abram left Haran only after Terah died), and Gen 11:32 (Terah died at 205), then Abram was at least 135 when he left Haran — which would make Ishmael's birth even later than that, not at 86.
entries.commentary: This contradiction is a downstream consequence of the Terah chronology problem in id=55, and the same harmonization is in play: apologists like Bock argue Gen 11:26's 'Terah lived seventy years, and begat Abram' means Terah began his childbearing at 70 rather than that Abram was born when Terah was 70, so the 135-year figure dissolves. If you accept that reading, Gen 16:16's 86 is fine. But the same objection applies: the Shem genealogies in Gen 11:10-26 use the identical formula to give precise birth ages, and there is no principled reason to read it as 'age at first child' only at verse 26. Claus Westermann and Nahum Sarna both note that the formulaic pattern is consistent, and that the anomaly at Gen 11:26 is an artifact of the redactor wanting Abram listed first for theological reasons even if he wasn't the eldest. The Samaritan Pentateuch already adjusted Terah's lifespan to fix this — which tells you the contradiction was real enough to require emergency textual surgery. Acts 7:4 represents the Hellenistic Jewish tradition (Philo also reads Abram leaving Haran after Terah's death) taking the MT at face value and producing the chronology that conflicts with Gen 16:16. The apologetic fix works only by treating Gen 11:26 as uniquely non-literal in a formulaic context where every other instance is literal. That is the definition of ad hoc reasoning.

entries.question: Did God call Abraham before or after he moved to Haran?
entries.summary: Acts 7:2-3 has Stephen claim God appeared to Abraham in Mesopotamia, before he dwelt in Haran, and commanded him to leave his country. Genesis 11:31-12:4 has the family settle in Haran first, and then Yahweh speaks to Abram there, issuing the call from Haran — not from Mesopotamia before it.
entries.commentary: Bock and Bruce argue that Genesis 15:7 ('I am the LORD that brought thee out of Ur of the Chaldees') and Nehemiah 9:7 ('Thou art the LORD the God, who didst choose Abram, and broughtest him forth out of Ur') both point to an earlier, pre-Haran call that is logically implied but not narrated in Genesis 12. On that reading, Stephen is drawing on a legitimate broader Jewish tradition and Genesis 12 just restates the call. That's a serious argument. Philo, Josephus, and Jubilees all preserve variants of a pre-Haran call, so Stephen isn't inventing it. But the Genesis 12 narrative reads naturally as a call issued at Haran: Terah's family migrates from Ur toward Canaan but settles in Haran, Terah dies there, and then Yahweh speaks to Abram. The narrator gives no indication Abram had already received a command — Genesis 12:1 introduces it as a new divine word, not as a restatement. Fitzmyer and Pervo both treat Stephen's speech as drawing on Hellenistic Jewish traditions (Philo, Jubilees) that smooth the narrative gap left by Genesis, but those traditions are interpretive expansions, not the text of Genesis itself. So the contradiction holds at the level of the Genesis narrative as written — Stephen is harmonizing with extrabiblical Jewish tradition, and his harmonization flattens a real narrative seam.

entries.question: Can God be seen?
entries.books_in_tension: Genesis, Exodus, Numbers, Deuteronomy, Judges, 1 Kings, 2 Chronicles, Job, Psalms, Isaiah, Ezekiel, Amos, Habakkuk, Baruch, Matthew, John, Acts, Colossians, 1 Timothy, 1 John
entries.summary: The Hebrew Bible repeatedly narrates theophanies in which God is seen face-to-face — by Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, Moses, seventy elders, Manoah, Micaiah, Job, Isaiah, Ezekiel, Amos, Habakkuk. A parallel stream (Exod 33:20; John 1:18; 1 Tim 6:16; Col 1:15) insists God is invisible and cannot be seen, and that anyone who did see him would die. Scripture affirms both mutually exclusive positions without resolving them.
entries.commentary: The dominant harmonization, articulated by Kaiser, Carson, and most systematic theologians, is that the visible theophanies are either angelic mediators, the pre-incarnate Logos, or partial/accommodated manifestations — never the unmediated divine essence. That move was already underway in ancient Judaism: the Targums routinely substitute 'the Memra (Word) of the Lord' for YHWH in theophany scenes, and Philo systematically distinguishes God's essence from his visible powers. But that harmonization is a post-hoc theological grid imposed on texts that don't share it. Genesis 32:30 has Jacob explicitly say 'I have seen God face to face' and name the place Peniel ('face of God'); Exodus 24:10-11 has seventy elders 'see the God of Israel' and eat and drink in his presence without dying; Exodus 33:11 has Yahweh speak to Moses 'face to face, as a man speaketh to his friend.' These narratives are not written as guarded angelophanies — they're written as actual encounters with Yahweh. Mark Smith's The Origins of Biblical Monotheism and Benjamin Sommer's The Bodies of God both document that early Israelite religion assumed Yahweh had a visible form, and that the later invisibility tradition (especially in Deuteronomistic and Johannine theology) represents a theological development. Sommer's argument is specifically that the 'fluidity of divine embodiment' was not felt as a contradiction until later monotheizing theology made it one. The contradiction isn't within a unified theology — it's the archaeological record of a religion whose concept of God changed over a thousand years. Exodus 33:20 and Exodus 33:11 sit in the same chapter and cannot be harmonized into a single stable doctrine of divine visibility.

And the LORD appeared unto Abram, and said, Unto thy seed will I give this land: and there builded he an altar unto the LORD, who appeared unto him. Genesis 12:7

And when Abram was ninety years old and nine, the LORD appeared to Abram, and said unto him.... Genesis 17:1

And the Lord appeared unto him [Abrham] in the plains of Mamre. Genesis 18:1

And I [God] appeared unto Abraham. Exodus 6:3

And he said, Men, brethren, and fathers, hearken; The God of glory appeared unto our father Abraham, when he was in Mesopotamia, before he dwelt in Charran Acts 7:2


Isaac saw him twice.


And the LORD appeared unto him [Isaac], and said, Go not down into Egypt; dwell in the land which I shall tell thee of. Genesis 26:2

And the LORD appeared unto him [Isaac] the same night, and said, I am the God of Abraham thy father: fear not. Genesis 26:24

And I appeared unto ... Isaac. Exodus 6:3


Jacob saw God face to face and beat him in a wrestling match.


Thy name shall be called no more Jacob, but Israel: for as a prince hast thou power with God and with men, and hast prevailed. And Jacob called the name of the place Peniel: for I have seen God face to face, and my life is preserved. Genesis 32:30

And God appeared unto Jacob again, when he came out of Padanaram, and blessed him. Genesis 35:9

And Jacob said unto Joseph, God Almighty appeared unto me at Luz in the land of Canaan. Genesis 48:3

And I appeared unto ... Jacob. Exodus 6:3


Moses spoke to God face to face and even got a peek at God's backsides!


The LORD God ... appeared unto me [Moses], saying, I have surely visited you. Exodus 3:16

That they may believe that the LORD God ... hath appeared unto thee [Moses]. Exodus 4:5

And the Lord spake to Moses face to face, as a man speaketh to his friend. Exodus 33:11

My servant Moses is not so, who is faithful in all mine house. With him will I speak mouth to mouth, even apparently, and not in dark speeches; and the similitude of the LORD shall he behold. Numbers 12:7-1

And there arose not a prophet since in Israel like unto Moses, whom the Lord knew face to face. Deuteronomy 34:10

And I [God]will take away my hand, and thou [Moses] shalt see my backparts. Exodus 33:23


Moses, Aaron, Nadab, Abihu, and seventy elders saw God.


Then went up Moses and Aaron, Nadab and Abihu, and seventy of the elders of Israel. And they saw the God of Israel ... They saw God, and did eat and drink. Exodus 24:9-11


God talked face to face to all the people of Israel, and plans to do so again someday.


For they have heard that thou Lord art among this people, that thou Lord art seen face to face. Numbers 14:14

The Lord talked with you [the people of Israel] face to face in the mount out of the midst of the fire. Deuteronomy 5:4

Afterwards he was seen upon earth, and conversed with men. Baruch 3:38

And I [God] will bring you [the Israelites] into the wilderness of the people, and there will I plead with you face to face.Ezekiel 20:35


Manoah and his wife (Samson's parents) saw God. (Manoah thought God would kill them for it.)


And Manoah said unto his wife, We shall surely die, because we have seen God. But his wife said unto him, If the LORD were pleased to kill us, he would not have received a burnt offering and a meat offering at our hands, neither would he have shewed us all these things, nor would as at this time have told us such things as these. And the woman bare a son, and called his name Samson. Judges 13:22-24


Micaiah saw God sitting on his throne.


I [Micaiah] saw the Lord sitting on his throne, and all the host of heaven standing by him on his right hand and on his left. 1 Kings 22:19, 2 Chronicles 18:18


Job saw God after God and Satan tormented him and killed his children.


I have heard of thee by the hearing of the ear: but now mine eye seeth thee. Job 42:5


David saw God in the sanctuary.


To see thy power and they glory, so as I have seen thee in the sanctuary. Psalm 63:2
(Supposedly "A Psalm of David")


Isaiah, a man of unclean lips, saw God sitting on a throne below some six-winged seraphim.


I [Isaiah] saw, also, the Lord sitting upon a throne, high and lifted up, and his train filled the temple. Above it stood the seraphims: each one had six wings. ... Then said I, Woe is me! for I am undone; because I am a man of unclean lips, and I dwell in the midst of a people of unclean lips: for mine eyes have seen the King, the LORD of hosts. Isaiah 6:1-2


Ezekiel saw God's loins, which appeared to be on fire.


And I saw ... the appearance of his loins even upward, and from the appearance of his loins even downward, I saw as it were the appearance of fire, and it had brightness round about. ... This was the appearance of the likeness of the glory of the LORD. And when I saw it, I fell upon my face. Ezekiel 1:27-28


Amos saw God standing on a wall with a plumbline in his hand.


The LORD stood upon a wall made by a plumbline, with a plumbline in his hand. Amos 7:7

I saw the Lord standing upon the altar: and he said, smite the lintel of the door, that the posts may shake. Amos 9:1


Habakkuk saw horns coming out of God's hand.


God came from Teman, and the Holy One from mount Paran ... He had horns coming out of his hand. Habakkuk 3:3-5


And Jesus said that angels see God's face, and whoever has seen Jesus has seen God.


Take heed that ye despise not one of these little ones; for I say unto you, That in heaven their angels do always behold the face of my Father which is in heaven. Matthew 18:9

He that hath seen me hath seen the Father. John 14:9


No, God is invisible and cannot be seen. (And if you do see him, you'll die.)


There shall no man see me, and live. Exodus 33:20

No man hath seen God at any time. John 1:18, 1 John 4:12

And the Father himself, which hath sent me, hath borne witness of me. Ye have neither heard his voice at any time, nor seen his shape. John 5:37

Not that any man hath seen the Father. John 6:46

...the invisible God ... Colossians 1:15

Now unto the King eternal, immortal, invisible, the only wise God, be honor and glory for ever and ever. 1 Timothy 1:17

Whom no man hath seen nor can see. 1 Timothy 6:16

assessment.reasoning: Critical scholarship (Sommer, Smith, Hamori) reads the seeing-God theophanies and the invisibility texts as evidence of developmental change in Israelite conceptions of divine embodiment; Exod 33:11 and 33:20 sit in the same chapter and resist a single stable doctrine.

entries.question: When was the city of Dan named?
entries.summary: Genesis 14:14 narrates Abraham pursuing raiders 'unto Dan' — during the patriarchal age. Judges 18:29 states that the city was originally named Laish and was only renamed Dan after the Danite conquest of Laish, centuries after Abraham. The city cannot have borne the name 'Dan' during Abraham's lifetime.
entries.commentary: This is a textbook example of what biblical scholars call an anachronism — a later editorial insertion of a name that didn't yet exist at the narrative's chronological moment. The standard harmonization, offered by Kitchen and Archer, is that Gen 14:14's 'Dan' is either a scribal updating (a later copyist replacing an obsolete place-name with the then-current one so readers would recognize it) or a reference to a different, earlier Dan unrelated to the later Danite city. The scribal-updating explanation is actually the consensus critical view too — Alexander Rofé, Michael Fishbane, and Emanuel Tov all cite Gen 14:14 as one of the clearest examples of post-compositional onomastic updating in the Torah. That's not a harmonization that rescues inerrancy; it's an admission that the text was edited. Once you grant that later hands modernized place-names, you've conceded that the Pentateuch as we have it is not a verbatim Mosaic composition. Friedman, in Who Wrote the Bible?, uses precisely this kind of anachronism to argue for a post-Mosaic redaction layer. The apologetic move of 'it's just scribal updating' works as an explanation for the phenomenon but undermines the theological framework apologists usually want to preserve. The contradiction stands at the level of the text as a record of the patriarchal age.
entries.scholarship: Fishbane, Michael. Biblical Interpretation in Ancient Israel (Oxford, 1985), Part One on scribal comments and corrections (lexical/explicative glosses). Friedman, Richard Elliott. Who Wrote the Bible?, 2nd ed. (HarperOne, 1997), on Pentateuchal anachronisms and post-Mosaic redaction. Rofé, Alexander. Introduction to the Composition of the Pentateuch (Sheffield Academic, 1999), on editorial insertions. Tov, Emanuel. Textual Criticism of the Hebrew Bible, 3rd ed. (Fortress, 2012), on onomastic updating. Na'aman, Nadav. Ancient Israel's History and Historiography: The First Temple Period, Collected Essays vol. 3 (Eisenbrauns, 2006), collected essays on Israel's historical geography and First-Temple-period historiography.

answers.answer_explanation:
And when Abram heard that his brother was taken captive, he armed  his trained servants, 
				        born in his own house, three hundred and eighteen, and pursued them unto Dan. 
				        Genesis 14:14

And they called the name of the city Dan, after the name of Dan their father, 
				        who was born unto Israel: howbeit the name of the city was Laish at the first. 
				        Judges 18:29

assessment.reasoning: Gen 14:14's 'Dan' is the consensus critical example of post-compositional onomastic updating/anachronism (Fishbane, Rofé, Tov); the name did not exist in the patriarchal period per Judges 18:29, and 'scribal updating' concedes rather than removes the anachronism.
